title: edge-case-taskflows-customer-synthesis-mar2026
body:
Executive summary:

This note synthesizes findings from six moderated usability sessions focused on low-frequency but high-impact taskflows in the Redwood Console. The emphasis was on three edge scenarios that we suspect drive support volume and operational risk: 1) model fallback and quality regression handling, 2) credentialing + private deployment onboarding, 3) quota exhaustion and cost/latency troubleshooting. Sessions were run with a mix of existing Dedicated customers and prospects evaluating Private. Goal: identify friction, produce annotated wireframe adjustments, and create a groomed backlog with acceptance criteria and rough effort buckets.

Key takeaways (high level):
- Users expect consistent, first-class error surfaces: they treat model fallback as a deliberate product decision and want transparent, actionable signals (why this model, how to revert, quality impact).
- Onboarding to Private+VPC is perceived as risky — even technical buyers want a concise checklist and progress telemetry in the Console.
- Quota and cost incidents are confusing: customers conflate token quotas, per-request rate limits, and dedicated capacity burst behaviors. Quick triage widgets (live usage, recent spikes, sample request inspection) would reduce support tickets.

Research setup:
- Format: 6 sessions, 45 minutes each, remote moderated. Prompted tasks + think-aloud.
- Participants: 2 platform engineers from mid-market SaaS, 2 ML engineers from AI-native startups, 2 infra/ops leads from enterprise prospects evaluating Private.
- Prototype: mid-fidelity wireframes in Figma (console flows for model fallback, private onboarding wizard, quota inspector).
- Notable constraints: sessions used non-production dataset and mocked backend responses for fallbacks. We focused on UI/UX rather than infra provisioning time.

Scenarios tested (task list):
1) Model fallback investigation: user is alerted that a recent rollout caused degraded outputs for a key route. Tasks: inspect the rollout history, compare outputs for two model versions, manually promote previous model as a fallback.
2) Private deployment onboarding: user must register a new Private deployment, connect their VPC, upload KMS info, and validate connectivity. Tasks: follow onboarding wizard, interpret validation failures, find next steps for network/security.
3) Quota & cost incident: user notices a spike in per-hour token consumption. Tasks: find which routes/models generated the spike, throttle or rollback traffic, and configure a daily quota alert.

Top observations (detailed):
A. Model fallback & rollout visibility
- Pain: rollout metadata is terse. Users repeatedly asked for a clear diff between model variants: token-level cost delta, known-issue flags (e.g., hallucination risk), and sample-output comparisons.
- Quote: "I don’t want to guess which model made this change — show me a side-by-side on a canonical prompt."
- Behavior: when sample-comparison was available in the prototype, participants used it first and cited it as decisive for rollback.
- UI fix (wireframe note): Add an expandable sample-output pane in the rollout details with diff highlights and metadata badges (latency delta, cost / 1k tokens, quantization level).

B. Private deployment onboarding friction
- Pain: long, opaque validation steps (e.g., "waiting for VPC route to be reachable") made participants unsure whether progress was happening or if action was required on their side.
- Quote: "Is it stuck? Did I misconfigure the firewall? The Console should tell me exactly what to check."
- Behavior: participants scanned logs then jumped to docs; when a checklist with links to targeted docs was present, confidence increased.
- UI fix: Convert the free-text status area into a stepper with explicit next actions, estimated time, and one-click copyable commands for network teams. Show last validation timestamp and link to a lightweight diagnostic download (zip of checks).

C. Quotas, rate limits & cost triage
- Pain: users conflate quota exhaustion (hard limit), rate-limiting (throttles), and temporary Dedicated burst behavior (soft limit). The Console uses separate pages for usage analytics and rate-limit config, which confused users during incident response.
- Quote: "Why did my requests start getting 429s and then later succeed? Is it caching? throttling? Something else?"
- Behavior: The single-pane incident inspector we tested (shows timeline of 429s, model switches, and route throttle settings) was the most helpful artifact.
- UI fix: Create an incident timeline widget that overlays token usage, 429 events, model fallback events, and capacity autoscaling events. Provide a quick-action to pause routes or pin an older model.

Edge-case micro-interactions observed:
- Users expect copyable CLI snippets next to validation errors for Private onboarding (curl / terraform equivalents).
- When rollback is a single click, users feel empowered but also want an "audit-and-confirm" affordance that preserves the rollout record; propose a lightweight modal that requires brief justification.
- Inline sample diffs should allow filtering by prompt tags and by user-provided failing examples.

Annotated wireframe notes (from Figma prototype):
- Rollout details panel: add header badges: {model-variant, quantized, seq-len-target}. Under the header, a two-column sample diff. Under that, a small metrics row: latency P50/P95, cost delta (%), estimated tokens per request.
- Private onboarding stepper: steps = {Provision, Network validation, KMS validation, Smoke-run}. Each step has: status icon, elapsed time, expected duration, one-click commands, and an expandable log.
- Quota incident inspector: timeline at top, table of top 10 routes by token consumption, and a filter for "suspicious bursts" (requests > 5x average). Quick actions on each route: throttle (60s/5m), pin-model, archive-samples.

Groomed backlog (prioritized):
1) Incident timeline widget (P0)
- Why: reduces support tickets and speeds triage.
- Acceptance criteria: timeline surfaces token usage, 429s, model variant changes; supports zoom into 1h/24h/7d; quick actions to throttle route and pin model.
- Rough estimate: 2 sprint frontend + 1 sprint backend integration.

2) Rollout sample-diff view + audit rollback modal (P0)
- Why: users used sample diffs to decide rollbacks; need audit trail.
- Acceptance criteria: side-by-side sample compare, diff highlights, rollback modal captures user reason and links to rollout record.
- Rough estimate: 1 sprint frontend + 1 sprint API change.

3) Private onboarding stepper + diagnostic bundle (P1)
- Why: reduces uncertainty and support back-and-forth with network teams.
- Acceptance criteria: stepper present for Private deployments, each step contains targeted next steps and copyable CLI commands; diagnostic bundle downloadable.
- Rough estimate: 2 sprints (frontend + small infra helper).

4) Quota/limit glossary & contextual help (P2)
- Why: prevent confusion between quota types.
- Acceptance criteria: inline help tooltips for quota/limit settings; searchable glossary; linkable to support playbooks.
- Rough estimate: 1 sprint content + 0.5 sprint frontend.

5) Sample set tagging & filtering (P2)
- Why: users asked to filter diffs by canonical prompts and failing examples.
- Acceptance criteria: UI to tag prompts, filter sample diffs by tag, export selected samples.
- Rough estimate: 1 sprint.

Open questions / trade-offs:
- How much real-time telemetry do we want in the Console versus directing users to exported diagnostics? Real-time reduces uncertainty but increases backend load and complexity.
- Rollback audit friction: one-click rollback speeds recovery but may be misused; do we require SSO-based 2FA for rollbacks in Dedicated/Private?
- Scope for incident timeline: should it pull autoscaling events from infra teams or only Redwood runtime events?

Immediate next steps:
- Design will produce high-fidelity mocks for the Incident Timeline and Rollout sample-diff by Mar 20.
- PM to open JIRA epics for P0 items and schedule spike to validate backend telemetry availability.
- Schedule a follow-up lab with three past customers who reported production incidents to validate the incident timeline assumptions (target: Apr 1).

Appendix: raw session snippets (verbatim where useful)
- Participant M1 (platform eng): "If I can see a canonical failing prompt and the before/after I can patch the route without emailing support."
- Participant S2 (ML eng): "Private onboarding needed a checklist I can hand to our SRE team — they don’t want to click around the Console to find logs."
- Participant E1 (infra lead): "I hit a 429 spike once and then it silently recovered — I have no idea what happened in between."

Notes to implementation partners:
- Backend needs to persist sample comparisons per rollout; avoid on-the-fly diff generation at render time for 7d+ histories. Consider a job that materializes canonical diffs for the last N rollouts.
- Instrumentation: mark fallback events explicitly in logs so the timeline can aggregate them without heuristic matching.

This doc is intentionally pragmatic: focus on small, high-impact UI surfaces that reduce support load and empower customers to triage. Use the grooming items above to create finer-grained tickets.

Prepared by: Aisha Malik (Product PM)
Reviewed by: Ethan Cole, María Alvarez, Samir Patel

Last updated: 2026-03-11

End of doc.
